name: Hydrogen
extract_html: Hydrogen is the universe's ultimate building block. Sitting at the very beginning of the periodic table with atomic number 1, it is the lightest, simplest, and most abundant element in existence. In fact, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter! Most of the hydrogen in our universe was forged just minutes after the Big Bang, meaning the hydrogen atoms in your body are nearly 13.8 billion years old. On Earth, hydrogen is almost never found floating freely as a gas. Instead, it loves to team up with other elements, most famously bonding with oxygen to create the water (H2O) that covers our blue planet. In its pure form, hydrogen is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic, and highly flammable gas. Across cultures, its life-giving nature is recognized: in several Indian languages, it is called "Jala-janaka" or "Udajani," which beautifully mirrors its Greek name by also meaning "the creator of water."

sections.Isotopes: Hydrogen is unique among the elements because its three naturally occurring isotopes have their own special names! The most common is Protium (Hydrogen-1), which accounts for over 99.98% of all hydrogen. Its nucleus is incredibly simple: just a single proton and no neutrons. The second isotope is Deuterium (Hydrogen-2). It has one proton and one neutron. Most of the universe's deuterium was created during the Big Bang. When deuterium replaces protium in water molecules, it forms what scientists call "heavy water," which is commonly used in modern nuclear reactors—like those operating in India's Kalpakkam facility. The third isotope, Tritium (Hydrogen-3), has one proton and two neutrons. Tritium is radioactive and glows in the dark! While rare, it is used in self-powered lighting devices like the glowing dials on high-end watches and in cutting-edge nuclear fusion research.
sections.History: The discovery of hydrogen is a fascinating tale spanning both ancient philosophy and modern chemistry. Long before modern science, ancient Indian philosophers like Kanada developed sophisticated theories of paramanu (indivisible atoms). Some modern interpretations of ancient Indian texts, like the Agastya Samhita, even point to descriptions of early battery-like setups using copper and zinc that could theoretically split water into oxygen and hydrogen gases! In Western science, the Swiss-German alchemist Paracelsus noticed a highly flammable gas bubbling from metals in acids during the 1500s. Fast forward to 1766, and British scientist Henry Cavendish officially isolated the gas by mixing zinc with hydrochloric acid, calling it "flammable air" and proving it created water when burned. In 1788, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it the modern name, Hydrogen, combining the Greek words hydro (water) and genes (creator).
sections.Occurrence: In the vastness of space, hydrogen is the undisputed king. It fuels the stars, including our Sun, where it constantly undergoes nuclear fusion to create helium, radiating the light and heat that makes life on Earth possible. It also forms the massive swirling clouds of gas deep in space and makes up the bulk of giant planets like Jupiter and Saturn. But on Earth, hydrogen tells a different story. Because it is so wonderfully light, any unattached hydrogen gas floated away into space billions of years ago. Today, almost all the hydrogen on our planet is locked away in chemical partnerships. It is a vital part of water, fossil fuels, and every living organism. Interestingly, geologists are now discovering rare pockets of "white hydrogen" trapped deep underground, naturally created when water reacts with iron-rich rocks or radioactive minerals!
sections.Applications: Hydrogen is rapidly becoming a superstar in the global quest for clean, green energy. While traditionally used to refine petroleum and manufacture fertilizers, its future lies in saving the planet. Because hydrogen only produces water when burned or used in a fuel cell, it is the ultimate zero-emission energy carrier. Today, hydrogen fuel cells are powering buses, long-haul trucks, and even trains—in fact, Indian Railways is actively testing hydrogen-powered passenger coaches! India is aggressively pursuing this frontier through the National Green Hydrogen Mission, aiming for energy independence by 2070. Breakthroughs are happening fast: institutions like the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) are turning biomass into green hydrogen, while IIT Guwahati and the Centre for Nano and Soft Matter Sciences (CeNS) are perfecting ways to split water directly using just sunlight. From powering NASA rocket engines to flying pollution-free airplanes of the future, hydrogen is truly the fuel of tomorrow.
